extracted.intended_audience: students of aesthetics, philosophers, and creative writers who describe human beauty and gesture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic distinctions for depicting/assessing human beauty, grace, and expressive movement (architectonic vs mimic features; voluntary vs sympathetic movements; moral causes of grace). Useful for aesthetic analysis or realistic character description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectonic beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The visible expression of a rational conception: a fixed beauty supplied by nature (the execution of an intelligence's design) and calculable relative to the technique of the structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectonic beauty is produced where necessary natural laws are sustained by a teleological principle; it is 'fixed' and determined by nature's execution of the design. It may surpass other beauties in degree but is of the same kind. This beauty is primarily the work of nature (or 'the author of nature') rather than of the person, and it has its own lifecycle (blossoming, maturity, decline) largely unaffected by the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace (as person-determined beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is 'the beauty of the form under the influence of free will' — the beauty of phenomena that the person himself determines (a personal merit rather than a mere gift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace is contrasted with architectonic beauty: the former honors the person who possesses it, the latter honors nature's author. Grace issues from the interplay of moral freedom and sensuous manifestation; it is typically found in movement but can appear in repose if that repose is the result of habitual movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace arises in movement (and habitually in repose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace can be found only in movement, since modifications of the soul are manifested sensuously as movement; immobility may also possess grace if it is the durable trace of frequently repeated movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or judging grace, look for movement qualities (pace, rhythm, undulation) or stable postures that are the result of habitual, repeated graceful actions. Stillness that originated as frequent movement can carry grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between voluntary (intentional) and sympathetic (involuntary) movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary (intentional) movements are caused by will aimed at an end; sympathetic (involuntary) movements accompany a sentiment and are expressions of moral sensibility rather than physical instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary movement expresses the aim (the substance of the will) but not the form (the disposition); sympathetic movements, even if involuntary, manifest dispositions and are therefore central to revealing character and producing grace. When analyzing a movement, separate what is intentionally designed from what accompanies it as expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace depends on the involuntary/sympathetic element within movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely voluntary movements, not linked to any sympathetic (involuntary) element, cannot present grace; grace presupposes a disposition of the soul that colors movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In description or performance, leave parts of a movement 'undetermined' by intention (tone, slowness/rapidity, degree of force) so that moral sensibility can determine them — that undetermined portion is where grace appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance of effortlessness / ease is essential to grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense considers ease to be the first requisite of grace; neither the will nor passion should act as a constraining force upon physical nature for beauty to result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid portraying movements as forced, strained, or visibly disciplined; instead emphasize smoothness, natural rhythm, and the absence of tension. Constraint betrays artifice and destroys grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: True grace must appear involuntary; theatrical/imitative grace is an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: True grace ought to be pure nature or at least appear so; imitative or learned (theatrical) grace is a pendant to artificial beauty and will eventually betray intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of 'theatrical grace' — practiced poses, exaggerated mimicry, or cosmetic artifice (rouge, pads, false ringlets) that imitate grace: these may fool unpractised senses but lead to discovery, indifference, contempt, or disgust in a discerning observer. Naturalness must be preserved or convincingly simulated as unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking (mimic) features vs dumb (architectonic) features
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking features are physical phenomena that accompany and express states of the soul (mimic traits); dumb features are the fixed, plastic results of nature's work and do not express the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For character-expression, emphasize mimic/speaking features (gestures, looks, blushing, smiles) since these reveal moral states. Recognize that boundaries between speaking and dumb traits are fuzzy: long moral activity can alter fixed features, and plastic nature can resist change.

rubrics_metrics.name: To know a person's true character, attend to their mimic expression and gestures rather than their words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words reveal the character a person desires to have attributed to them; mimic expressions and involuntary gestures reveal the real character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing or analysis, give weight to involuntary gestures, facial micro-expressions, and spontaneous mimicry as evidence of authentic moral disposition. Use these as more reliable signals than deliberate speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faces that lack mimic expression indicate moral inertia or rule-bound existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat, inexpressive physiognomies indicate a mind that has made itself 'the punctual major-domo of physical nature', a sluggish soul that lets plastic nature work undisturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying characters who have repressed moral activity or lead mechanical lives, emphasize the absence of mimic traits and a dominance of architectonic (fixed) features; this absence itself is an expressive sign (leading to lack of perceived 'soul').

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between sensuous and rational parts is the ideal condition for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Three relations are possible: (1) reason suppresses sensuous nature (constraint), (2) sensuousness subjugates reason (animality), (3) harmony/accord between the two. The third yields the best expression and constitutes the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to depict or judge characters whose bodily expression shows an easy concord between appetite and reason: neither forced repression nor slavish indulgence, but a balance where moral dispositions facilitate the sensuous conditions of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disposition can (and should) bring about the sensuous conditions of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral cause (the state of the mind) can, in a necessary manner, prescribe to physical nature its accompanying state so that moral perfection produces the natural conditions favorable to beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating graceful characters, align their inner moral state with outward physical comportment: the right moral sentiments make natural ease and proportion more likely. Treat grace as the conjunction of a super-sensuous cause (moral) and a sensuous effect (natural beauty), not as purely one or the other.
